newsitem.title: USA: Chicago city council defers Swiss boycott proposal.
newsitem.headline: Chicago city council defers Swiss boycott proposal.

text.p: A Chicago City Council Committee deferred action Friday on an ordinance requiring local banks doing business with the city to sever financial ties to the gvernment of Switzerland or Swiss banks.

Following a two hour public hearing that included testimony from Holocaust survivors, the ordinance sponsors moved to table it to avoid any delays in Swiss authorities distributing aid through a humanitarian fund in the short term and an accounting over the next several years.

"I would not want to muddy the waters and to do something today that would stop payment of money (due Holocaust survivors and the heirs of victims)," Ald. Burton Natarus said. "I know this council is capable of acting and I know it could pass a boycott in 24 hours."

The public hearing also included testimony from a representative of the Swiss Bankers Association, the director of the Jewish Community Relations Council and the director of the midwest regional office of the American Jewish Committee.
Natarus, who sponsored the ordinance along with Ald. Bernard Stone, said holding it in the finance committee should be seen "not as a sign of weakness, but as a sign of strength."
Chicago will not wait another 52 years to act if some movement is not seen, added Ald. Ed Burke, finance committee chairman.
Natarus and Stone had originally included Swiss businesses in their proposal, but offered an amended ordinance on Friday directed at the Swiss government and Swiss banks only.

Michael Kotzin, Jewish Community Relations Council director, told the committee it would be right for local governments to speak out, support the principle and "send a message of concern and watchfulness."

The Swiss Bankers Association registered opposition to the ordinance through representative Thomas Delaney, who said that Switzerland and Swiss banks have taken "decisive steps" toward resolving the issue and providing restitution.
A written submission from Eduard Jaun, consul general of Switzerland in Chicago, said that Swiss authorities share the concerns.

"I can assure you that the government of my country is firmly committed to tacke its past and address it in a compassionate way, taking into account our long-standing humanitarian tradition," Jaun's letter stated.

Jonathan Levine, director of the midwest region for the American Jewish Committee, told the committee that while he found the Swiss government's conduct "appalling," he wanted no delays in the issuance of humanitarian aid to the remaining Holocaust survivors.

The ordinance was patterned after another directed at South Africa as a measure opposing Apartheid, which also included a prohibition against businesses. It was introduced in February and the sponsors made an introductory presentation four weeks ago to the finance committee.

Under the proposal, banks serving as depositories of city funds would be required to certify whether they have outstanding prohibited loans and, if so, to certify that they will not make future loans until the claims of Holocaust victims have been addressed.

The banks would also be required to certify that they are liquidating the loans, will complete the process within one year and will not convert any outstanding loans to longer maturity dates than those they presently hold.
The ordinance would not apply if the city comptroller determined that no eligible bank could perform the necessary function or if Chicago would incur significant financial losses.
